# sta310

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/eribul/STA310/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/eribul/STA310/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Package documentation](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-eribul.github.io%2FSTA310%2Fsta310-blue)](https://eribul.github.io/STA310/sta310/)
<!-- badges: end -->

`sta310` collects the data sets that accompany Collett (2023), *Modelling
Survival Data in Medical Research* (4th edition), together with a small set of
teaching functions that implement the estimators used in the STA310 course at
the University of Gothenburg from first principles. The estimators are written
so that the individual steps can be inspected in the lectures and computer
exercises, and they agree with the established implementations in `survival` to
within numerical tolerance.

## Installation

The package lives in the `sta310/` directory of the course repository, so
`subdir` has to be given:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
devtools::install_github("eribul/STA310", subdir = "sta310")
```

## Data sets

All 33 data sets from the book are available under the object names used in the
course material, with the original column names, and each of them has a help
page with the background of the study, the coded variables and the relevant
examples in Collett (2023):

```{r}
library(sta310)
data(package = "sta310")$results[, "Item"]
```

The package also ships `scottish_mbc_cohort`, the synthetic Scottish metastatic
breast cancer cohort used in the first computer exercise. It is **not** from the
book: it comes from the teaching material of the Edinburgh Cancer Informatics
group, and that is what its help page documents (`?scottish_mbc_cohort`).

Note that six of the names are also used by the `survival` package, for data
sets that are not the same: `bladder`, `cgd`, `kidney`, `myeloma`, `ovarian` and
`rats`. Attach `sta310` last, or use `sta310::myeloma`, if both packages are
attached.

```{r}
iud
```

## Teaching functions

* `km_estimate()` and `plot_km()`: the Kaplan-Meier estimator with Greenwood
  standard errors, and a plot of it.
* `cox_fit()`: Cox regression fitted by Newton-Raphson, with Breslow or Efron
  handling of ties.
* `emp_hazard()`: empirical, piecewise constant hazard estimates.
* `n_events_logrank()`, `power_logrank()` and `power_logrank_sim()`: sample
  size, power and simulation for the log-rank test.
* `cif_cause_specific()`: cumulative incidence functions from cause-specific
  Cox models.

## Example

`km_estimate()` returns the risk sets, the events and censorings, the survivor
function and its standard error at each event time:

```{r}
km <- km_estimate(iud$time, iud$status)
km
```

`cox_fit()` reproduces `survival::coxph()` on the same data:

```{r}
fit <- cox_fit(myeloma$time, myeloma$status, myeloma[, c("age", "bun")])
ref <- survival::coxph(survival::Surv(time, status) ~ age + bun, data = myeloma)
cbind(cox_fit = coef(fit), coxph = coef(ref))
```

See `vignette("sta310")` for a walk-through of the data sets and the teaching
functions, and `vignette("cs1-survival-analysis")` for the first computer
exercise, which has the solutions to all its questions hidden behind
*Show solution*. Both are HTML documents. The same material, with a complete
reference index, is online at <https://eribul.github.io/STA310/sta310/>.

## Course material

The lectures, exercises and labs that use this package are part of the same
repository. Collett (2023) is the textbook for the course:

> Collett, D. (2023) *Modelling Survival Data in Medical Research*, 4th ed.
> Chapman & Hall/CRC.
